utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I see Mr. Naletilic is not present at this moment. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are quite right, Your Honour. The registry has informed me that Mr. Naletilic does not feel well and cannot come. But we can continue without him. As you know, we have reached that understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then we'll continue with the proceedings. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness, I want to go over some of the matters you discussed yesterday in a bit more detail. What was the nature of your relationship, if any, with Mr. Martinovic, Stela, and with his family, before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were friends. We used to play together. We were good friends. There is a place in Balinovac where we all got together, all those pals from the area, playing football, sitting there chatting, and I've known him for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. When you say the two of you were friends and played together, you're talking about you and Stela personally; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were a number of us. Those were all the young guys from Balinovac. That was the place where we all got together, socialised.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During the war in 1993, after the time when you were released in about May 1993, did you continue to consider yourself to be close friends with Stela during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because as soon as I left the airport and I spent nine days there, I called him and he helped me and did everything for me, gave me some money, took me home, said, "Don't worry. Everything will be fine."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And since the war ended, and we'll just say roughly since the Dayton Agreement in 1995, do you consider yourself to continue to be friends with Mr. Martinovic, to the present time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I want to direct your attention, please, to the 9th of May, the day that you say, if I heard you correctly, you were arrested. Will you tell us a bit more about how it was that you came to be arrested? They came to your house and took you out, or can you just describe for us a bit more how it was that you were taken into custody.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened in the morning, around half past 5.00 or 6.00 on the 9th of May. There was a lot of gunfire, and I dressed to go out and see where was this happening, because I was in a room with my mother. And as I was about to open the door, when some soldiers turned up, must have forced me to get out of the house and directed me towards the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said just now that it was about half past 5.00 or 6.00 that you heard, presumably what sounded like fighting, gunshots or artillery, and you got up and got dressed. Approximately how long after 5.30 or 6.00 that morning were you then taken into custody by these soldiers? Was it a half hour later, two or three hours later? As best you can recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They simply drove us out of the house and took us to the stadium, to the Velez Stadium. That is where they took us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm asking you at the moment about the timing. How soon after you woke and dressed yourself did these soldiers come and take you away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was right before the daybreak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you were taken to the Velez stadium and then can you give the Judges some idea of the number of people? Obviously nobody expects you to give a precise number, but what did you see when you got to the Velez stadium? Approximately how many other people were gathered there at that time? Excuse me, Witness. Excuse me, Witness. We may be having some technical problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The French booth is asking the witness to come closer to the microphone. That is it. Could the witness please come closer to the microphone. This was the request from the French booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. Let me repeat my question. When you were taken to Velez Stadium that morning, approximately how many other people such as yourself had been gathered there when either at the time you first arrived or perhaps in the course of the time that you were held there, before being taken anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite a lot of people. They were coming. I don't know how many. Two hundred, 150. I guess people were coming and going.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how was it that people were then taken from the stadium? What arrangements did you see in place in terms of taking people from the stadium or pitch to someplace else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was taken away in a bus to the Ero Hotel, and I spent one night there, and in the morning they again put us on buses and took us to the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you were at the Velez Stadium still, approximately how many of these buses did you see there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were coming in twos, sometimes one by one, one at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you were held, then, for a time, or at least one night, you said, at the Ero Hotel, and then were you taken the next day to the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I want to direct your attention forward to the first part of July in 1993. What were you doing around that time, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1993, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If it assists you, I think, as I mentioned yesterday in another context, I think there will be agreement that there were two substantial instances of arrest, large-scale arrest, first in May and then again at the 1st of July. So I'm referring -- if it assists your memory, sir, I'm referring to the events in early July, when there were another -- there was another set or sequence of arrests. And if you could recall for us, please, what you were doing around that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm not even trying to say that cross-examination could be as short as my direct examination. However, I know -- perhaps it may sound strange, that the witness for the Defence is a Bosniak Muslim testifying in favour of my client. However, in the direct examination, this witness testified about specific points that the Defence has set out to prove. This is not a witness for the Prosecution to prove something that the Prosecution has already tried to prove, that there was some waves of persecution, or something. And I believe that the Prosecution should focus on what was covered by the direct examination of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President -- sorry. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the question asked by -- in the cross-examination is not necessarily confined within the scope of the direct examination, and we believe that those questions asked by the Prosecution are relevant to this case, and we are also interested to hear the answer from this witness as for those details. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, again, all I'm trying to do is assist you in focusing on a particular period of time. If you can recall to the early part of July 1993, what were you doing in Mostar around that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at home, hiding. I didn't go out at all. You know what it was like in Mostar. There were troops there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why were you hiding in early July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what do I know? Because they were coming there all the time, and I didn't want to be taken away again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, who was coming all the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were passing through, troops, I mean, soldiers, and they were rounding up people and taking them to the Heliodrom. And I went only once to the base, to Stela's, to ask him, but he said, "No, no, no. Don't worry. Go home, but stay there and there will be no problem."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. So perhaps we've established you stayed in your home in early July, but were you looking out the windows? Were you seeing what was happening? What did you see happening at that time, as you say, when all these people were coming to collect people? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I saw? I simply saw troops passing by. I was on the outskirts. I wasn't in the centre. They didn't come much to where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat, please? I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. You said they didn't come primarily to -- or mostly to the area that you were, and my question was: Why not? What was it about your area, the place where you lived, that would cause them not to come there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why they didn't come often. How can I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Judges, please: When did you first have contact with anyone about the possibility of appearing as a witness here for Mr. Martinovic, Stela?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I watched television and media, and in the media I saw these indictments against Vinko Martinovic, Stela, and I went right away to Vinko Martinovic's father and his brother and said, "If you ever need anything, to testify for Stela, count me as number one." Why? Because he was good to me when I needed it most, when my mother died, and one does not forget that, and I'll never forget it as long as I live. And he also helped me. I survived. So I said, "Whatever may be necessary, whatever I can do, I'll go. I'll even walk there, if need be." Because he was very good to me, and I will never forget it. He helped me and my family and everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So when you say "after the indictment" you saw something on television after the indictment, you're saying sometime in early 1998? When did you see this and when did you go to the Martinovic family to offer your assistance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: 2000. 2000. If necessary, I will go. Perhaps a little earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you went to the Martinovic residence to communicate this information; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went there, and I went to Jadranko's, Stela's brother, to his premises, and I said the same thing to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, turning to the time after you were released from the Heliodrom, again, it wasn't completely clear to me what your involvement was, if any, with Mr. Martinovic or his unit during the summer and fall of 1993. Now, you've told us you were a car electrician. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you perform electrical work, electrical repair work or other work on vehicles for Stela or his unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did now and then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, you say "now and then." Was that a frequent -- something you did frequently or would you say that in the summer, for example, of 1993 you might have only done it two or three times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: A number of times. I had my workshop there, and they always came to me to repair whatever was needed for them, because I was the only car electrician there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You say you had your workshop "there." Did you have a workshop somewhere near your residence or did you have a workshop at or near the Vinko Skrobo unit headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had my workshop in the house in which I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you do this work only for Stela and his unit or did you perform this electrical work, repair work, for other HVO units as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did it for other soldiers who came there. I couldn't -- whenever somebody came, I had to work for him, to repair it. One of them who came almost killed me. Had it not been for Vinko Martinovic, Stela, he would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Approximately how long, then, if we look through 1993 and thereafter, approximately how long, then, did you continue to provide your services to Stela and his unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked whenever necessary. I was there all the time. Whenever one of them came, I worked. I don't know about time. There was a war on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you ever -- apart from perhaps if it was on the occasion when you requested some assistance from Stela, were you ever at his headquarters on Kalemova Street. Were you ever at his headquarters more than once?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: At times, but not too often.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you ever at a place called the health centre, on the confrontation line in Mostar, during 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, sir, were you ever at the confrontation line, anywhere along the line, during the summer and fall of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Only once, when I had to switch on a car for one of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately where, what part of the confrontation line that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's before the line, over there, in Podhum. That area is called Podhum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. So it wasn't actually on a confrontation line itself, even on that particular occasion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. Yes, yes. You are quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, did you, when you were at the times -- excuse me. At the time when you may have been at Stela's headquarters or working at some other location, did you come to know any of the Muslim prisoners who were being held or brought to Stela's headquarters from time to time? Did you know any of those prisoners. Did you work with them, for instance, on car repair?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew, and they came to my place, to my house, that is, to my workshop, to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me mention a few names to you and see if you recall having worked with or known any of these individuals. Did you ever know a man named Admir Satanic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Edin Huskovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Huskovic in the context of, again, someone providing mechanical services to Stela and his unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Edin Huskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you know a man named Semir Redzic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could go to private session for a couple of these names, please, again out of an abundance of caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware of what was happening in connection with East Mostar during the summer and fall of 1993? For example, did you realise it was under siege?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I realised that, but I stayed at home. I didn't go anywhere. I knew there was a siege. There was a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was there not regular shelling and sniping going on into East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was shooting. I don't know. There were all kinds of things. There was shooting from both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, that food and water had been cut off from East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, what's the relevance of these questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, the ability, both the ability and the tendency or inclination whether this witness -- what this witness did observe or didn't observe and what he's willing to tell us and not tell us, and I don't want to argue it in front of the witness more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, the poor man, in common with many other Muslims during the war, was trying to stay alive, keep his head down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Absolutely, Judge Clark. No suggestion to the contrary. Again, as I said, to determine certain aspects, which I won't argue at the time unless Your Honours tell me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, before we move on, I'm required to put certain things to you, and I will ask you these in terms of: Were you ever aware or did you ever hear that Stela was involved in smuggling or moving civilians through the confrontation line or getting them out of Mostar in exchange for money?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that either Mr. Martinovic himself, Stela, or members of his unit, the ATG, were hiding Muslims and protecting them, and again in exchange for financial gain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever hear a discussion about there being so-called private prisoners that were being kept by the ATG to perform work as units with the military units or performing work privately for members of those units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never heard of that, never.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the final set of questions, going back to the time when you were arrested and released from custody. You told us -- you've told us now that you were arrested on the 9th of May, 1993, you were held for approximately nine days. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And so you were released sometime, approximately, around the 18th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges how it was that you were released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, I used to work at my workshop in my house as a private businessman. Many of my friends came to have their cars repaired. And when I came to the Heliodrom, one of my friends noticed me and they asked me, "How come you're here?" And then he said, "No problems. Just rest in peace." And he came the following day. He put me in his car and he brought me home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: He came -- sorry. This man came to you at the Heliodrom and then drove you away in his private car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was working at the Heliodrom. He was working there. He saw me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, did you understand -- perhaps you don't know, sir, but did Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you understand that this man talked to someone in authority or made arrangements to have you released from the Heliodrom, or are you telling the Judges that he just simply walked in, collected you, and drove away from the Heliodrom with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he noticed me down there in the Heliodrom during the daylight. He asked me, "How did you end up here?" And he said, "I'll see, either tonight or tomorrow, and I will arrange for you to be released," and he did that on the following day. Because he was a very good friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps we should go to private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in the open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I didn't seem to have a problem myself, so if it persists, of course let me know and we'll try to test it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, did you have any dealings around the time you were released with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: There's some problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Apparently, the technical booth, we're not getting transmission. Hello.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, about the time that you were released, either before you were released or after you were released, did you ever have any knowledge of or dealings with a man named Juka Prazina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you know whether there were any Muslim women being held at the Heliodrom during the time that you were being held during those nine days? Was it just men or did you see women as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were women.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were there any women there that you knew from your neighbourhood or that you knew in general, from Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you happen to see a woman there by the name of Vanesa Kapic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, at the time that you were still held there, before you were released, isn't it fair to say, sir, that various Muslims were being released from the Heliodrom on essentially a daily basis during this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You think, sir, that during this time period you were the only one that was released, the only Muslim prisoner who was released along the lines that you've described to us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask a couple more questions. Do you recall, for instance, were some of the Muslim prisoners released because they were friends of certain Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of cases where Muslim prisoners were released because they somehow were friends with Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I haven't heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you hear of any Muslim prisoners being released because someone gave something called a "guarantee" for them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear any of these things. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me not use the word "guarantee." Did you understand that any of the Muslim prisoners had been released because someone had paid money to have them released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, it's been said in this courtroom that words to the effect, if not the exact quote - I don't want to be accused of misquoting it, but words to the effect that "everyone had his Muslims." If you can, sir, what does that phrase mean to you, or have you heard anything like that said before?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that it's really not necessary that I make an objection. This question, as much as it requires speculation, it even asks the witness to state who said what and what they thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No. No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution asked the witness whether he has ever heard anything like that said before. If the witness has not heard anything, he can say no. Let's hear the answer from this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if anyone gave anything. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, let me repeat my question, in light of the intervention. Around the time that you were being held, sir, or in this time generally, in the summer of 1993, or during these terrible events of what was happening in Mostar on all sides, did you hear anything use the phrase anything like: "Everyone had his Muslims"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like the witness to please be shown -- Mr. President, the Chamber may note, and counsel may note, that I have in fact skipped over a number of possible exhibits, but I will only use one, and that will be my last set of questions. Exhibit P401.1, which is one of the bundles -- yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I've handed you this document, and there is, I can see from here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received this just now. My colleague started yesterday with cross-examination, and I could have received this before the session. I don't think there was any problem, any obstacle with that. This is a principled objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Honourable Chamber, if the honourable Prosecutor could please explain where this came from. There is no signature. There is no seal. It could have come from anywhere. I'm sorry that I didn't do that during cross-examination. However, we still have to learn all the time in this court. I could have written this myself and then claim that it has been given to me by the government of Croatia, by the secret service of the Croatian people, just like the Prosecutor is doing. Can we know what is the foundation? Who wrote this? From whose notebook this came? Honourable Judge, I see that you are shaking your head, and I'm very disappointed. My question is very clear. But maybe I lack knowledge. I want to know who wrote this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think the president has something to say to you, Mr. Krsnik, now. You're really on thin ice. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone Judge Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry. We're going to have to start imposing fines or something, but I think Judge Liu has something to say to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, first of all, as to the use of the documents, this is our answer to Mr. Seric, that made a ruling that in the cross-examination, if possible, those documents used in the proceedings should be furnished to the Chamber and to the other parties. But sometimes it's very difficult to prejudge the outcome of cross-examination. There may be some questions in the answer of the witness that need some document. I think you are even luckier than us, because I haven't got that document myself yet. Mr. Krsnik, let's hear the answer from this witness. If you have some difficulties with these documents, you are entitled to raise this issue during the admission of this document, but we would not like to delay the proceedings on debating the authenticity of this document at this moment, and you should not stand up repeatedly on the same issue. Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if I can direct your attention, please, to the top of the first page of the Croatian language version, and I think I can see from here that you have that. You see the first four names, and there is a -- well, we should probably go to private session, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'm intrigued by some of your evidence, because you described before the war a very happy integration of the ethnic groups in your part of Mostar. Has that friendship continued to the present day? Do the groups still mix with the same degree of friendship as they did before the war, in your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In mine, yes. Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: It's a pity that somebody in your neighbourhood doesn't go on television or radio and teach the rest of the former Yugoslavia the recipe, because it's wonderful to hear that for us, that there were people who got on so well before the war, during the war, and afterwards. It's refreshing to hear that, because it seems pretty unique.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, life was fine, and we all lived together, and nobody bothered to know who or what is the next one. We lived together, worked together, drank together. Nobody ever asked about anyone's origins. Now it's a little bit different, but it is getting better. I have my neighbours, and we're all fine, and we're talking nicely, and nobody holds any grudges against anyone. That is how it is in the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could lead on to something else. You described how, before the war, you had your job, you had your little workshop at the house, and you lived with your mother. Did your brother also live with you and share the same trade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brother worked for a company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking you this, Mr. Witness, is that I'm curious as to know why somebody who lived with his mother in her room and had obviously a good position would suddenly find himself, when in the tragic situation of the death of his mother, being unable to pay for the funeral. Were your funds taken from you during the nine days of your incarceration?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I came I didn't have a lot of money. One had to have money to eat, to drink something. One needed to have something. So I didn't have money. There was the Serb war, then the war between Croats and Muslims, and whatever money one had was spent, and there wasn't much work. One couldn't really earn much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I see. Now, in relation to your workshop, you -- in translation - and I don't know whether this was a direct translation of what you said - you described how you had to keep your workshop open; you were at your workshop every day; you had to do it. Was there some compulsion on someone's part for you to be there at your workshop just in case any work was needed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No compulsion, but I needed something to live on. Somebody gave me this, somebody gave me that, and that is how you made your ends meet. Because I couldn't go anywhere. How could I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I go into private session for a minute, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Just arising out of that response, Mr. Witness: What made you go to Mr. Martinovic for protection in the first place? Is it because of your very close friendship with him or did you know that he was protecting other people in your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was friends with him before the war. We knew each other well. I trusted him, and I knew that he had not changed, and that is why I went to him, asking him for this favour. Because I knew that he would do it for me when I needed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that among your many friends and neighbours where you live, that people are really shocked at the accusations that have been levelled at Mr. Martinovic? Would that be a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than shocked. Half of Djikovina, all the Muslims that are there, he was the one who kept them there or returned. [redacted] [redacted] and they told me about that, how he brought them back from the medical school when others were forcing them to cross over to the other side. He was the one who sent them back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness, for your assistance, and I think that it would probably be a wise idea if we were to redact all those names that were mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Witness MH, I'd like to go back to the funeral. Is it that you had to pay for this funeral? Is it that your brother did not share in the expenses of this funeral? Because he works for a company. Didn't you share the expenses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could not. Nobody worked at the time. Nobody in any company worked. And he had two children and a wife, and nobody worked. So he probably had barely enough to survive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And other members of the Muslim community -- and how much did a funeral cost at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time nobody knew what were the prices. Whatever you had, you pay. And all I could, I paid 150 Croatian dinars for the coffin. And yes, I had to pay a hodza too, because he was also in dire straits. And all this money, it was Stela who gave it to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Muslim community, don't they contribute, the Muslim -- it is one of the Muslim customs that the whole community contributes, under normal circumstances.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an old woman, Mujesera. He paid my mother and prepared and dressed her. That was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judges' questions? Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Only one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: When Her Honour Judge Clark asked you and you said you had to work in order to make some money, when you worked for Vinko Martinovic, Stela, did he always pay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't wait for him to come, because he would always pay and overpay. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. That will be all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, Witness, for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. The usher will show you out of the room when he comes back and pulls down the blinds. We all wish you a pleasant journey back home and good business in the future.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The Defence has no documents to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would tender the map again, the P11/18.18, I should say, as marked by the witness. I don't know which number that .../18, I guess it is. And in addition to that, Your Honour, we would admit -- we would tender to the Chamber - excuse me - Exhibit P401.1. Anticipating, Mr. President, if I might be allowed to anticipate questions by -- objections by counsel, based on what's already been said: Your Honour, the original of the document will show, if you look at the Croatian version, on the upper right-hand corner, as the Chamber will recognise from this many months into this trial, the stamp of the Zagreb archive. I can further represent to the Chamber that it comes from the Zagreb archive. In addition to that, Mr. President, I think the witness gave additional indicia of authenticity. It is corroborated by the facts independently provided by the witness. It is indeed the date that he says he was released. He also recognised his brother's name on the document and gave us information about his brother's release. That would be consistent with the document. So we tender 401.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I have a question concerning this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It seems to me that it's just a part of a whole lot, a whole document. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wouldn't honestly be able to tell you that more than what's on the document. It appears to be a list of 56 names which -- excuse me, Mr. President. Sorry, Mr. President. The last page of my Croatian version is missing, the copy that I have, so I'm not able to ... Yes, that's what I remembered. Mr. President, I can only say that the last page, 56, ends at the top of the page. It doesn't appear to be -- I can only say it doesn't appear to be a continuing list, or presumably we would have 57, 58, et cetera, on that particular page. It appears to be a complete list of 56 names in itself, as far as I know, to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is this explanation satisfactory to the Defence counsel? Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence has no objections to the map which is tendered. As regards this document, Vinko Martinovic's Defence does not consider it a document at all, not only that the Prosecutor's answer is not satisfactory, but this is not a document at all, only after we get the integral document, the document from which this was taken, we shall be able to decide. So my first objection is that we do not have an integral text; secondly, we shall also need a certain period of time to respond, in writing, to the Prosecution's proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. First I wish to apologise for the manner in which I spoke. I did not really understand that I could not react instinctively, as my heart as a lawyer bids me to do, that is, that I'm not supposed to react to a document as soon as I see it. Because I think an intervention which is not timely means nothing, at least in my -- in the trade that I am engaged in. But I apologise, Your Honours. I was not -- it was not my intention to be rude. Your Honours, as for this document, we can also respond in writing. But I wish to tell you something sincerely. Perhaps my temperament, perhaps my emotions take the upper hand at time, because I truly don't know how to react any longer, and I only hope that truth will reach you, that you will recognise the truth. Your Honours, quite sincerely speaking, I could have written this. There. I think that that said, that suffices to show what kind of a document this is. Can it really be that in the courtroom of the World Tribunal for war crimes, pieces of paper can appear that we do not know where they come from, who wrote them, why he wrote them, for what reason he wrote them? We know nothing except that the Prosecutor says it comes from the archive, but again, he knows nothing either. Whether it comes from Mostar, whether it comes from Ljubuski, from Zagreb, from Sarajevo. Perhaps these people from incarcerated in Sarajevo. And this witness has practically invalidated this document because he said that nobody guaranteed for his brother, and here it says clearly that someone guaranteed my brother and the witness said, "No. My brother was released and nobody was released and nobody guaranteed for them." Even the dates, Your Honour, there's no need for me to go on any further. I believe that such wise people as you are need no further argument. But if necessary, we can argue it in writing. Of course, my indignation with the procedure that is being applied here, maybe I'll write a book and give vent to it there, but I do not wish to tax your patience any longer, because I'm really indignant that in the World Tribunal for war crimes, such pieces of paper are produced and called documents. I believe that the history of law will write about it. I think I'm fighting enough for certain things to show the direction in which future lawyers and future tribunals should go. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, in addition to what my lead counsel has just mentioned, and in addition to what Mr. Seric just mentioned, I believe we had the same situation when Mr. Bos from the Prosecution team was cross-examining a witness the other day. What's happening here is that the Prosecution is trying to bootstrap this document into evidence through the back door. Mr. Scott could have very easily asked a set of questions to this witness, without showing him the document. The witness, after having seen the document, answered every question in the negative, and yet, save and except for: Were you released on a certain date with some other prisoners? He had already admitted he was released around the 17th or 18th. However, in response to the question from Mr. Scott: Was Juka Prazina the commander of your friend? Or: Was your friend a soldier of Juka Prazina? No. Do you know if the approval of Mr. Naletilic was needed for your release? No. He could have asked that set of questions without putting this inflammatory document in front of Your Honours, and that's my additional objection. I thought we had this ironed out the other day. However, it appears - and we'll wait for your ruling, but it appears that the rules in this Trial Chamber change on an hourly and daily basis. I would just like to have a set ruling on how the Prosecution can go about trying to slip documents in the back door, through witnesses who have no knowledge of those documents, nor the contents of those documents, witnesses who could be asked simple questions. If they reply in the negative, there's no reason to show the document and try to have the document admitted. I believe it's highly improper, and I strongly object to this procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: No. I was just going to ask a question of the Prosecution, but I think that the Prosecution is entitled to respond to what you've said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Clark. Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, I'm not sure why we have to have three different counsel, not just two, but three different counsel arguing a point of law. Beyond that, Mr. President, I couldn't disagree more with what's been said. I think I respectfully submit that I handled the witness fairly. There was a moment when Judge Clark, I think, cautioned me a bit about perhaps being too rough and I think I took that advice into consideration and I hope I did to so the satisfaction of the Judge. But Your Honour, I asked a series of questions about his release and how it came that he was released, and nothing he said is inconsistent with the document. He said he didn't know who the soldier was. It was a soldier, someone who worked at the Heliodrom, either a soldier or a police officer. Did you know -- I think, and I can't go back now into the transcript, so I'm sure I'll be corrected if I'm wrong, but what I believe I heard the witness say is he didn't know what unit he was from, completely consistent with the possibility that it was in fact someone from Juka Prazina's unit. The document is consistent with otherwise what the testimony of the witness was. He quite, without any direction on my part -- the only question I put to the witness on the matter of his brother was: Would you please review the list and see if you recognise anyone else. Without any prompting from me or suggestion, he recognised his brother's name and indicated that indeed, indeed, he was released around this time. So I disagree with counsel on a number of respects. I also must register the strongest concern about the personal allegations that are being made. My personal good faith has been attacked, Mr. Bos's personal good faith has been attacked. I understand that counsel may not like this document. They may not like a lot of the Prosecution evidence. But when we have a witness come, and he gives us his name and talked about being held at the Heliodrom and being released on the 18th of May, 1993, and the Prosecutor has in his possession a document bearing the witness's name, bearing the date 18th of May, 1993, and then also obtains information about his brother, those are questions fairly put. How could counsel stand up and question the integrity of counsel of putting documents to the witness on that basis? So I object very much to the way that these objections are being made, and with all respect to counsel, I don't think it's an excuse to say: My emotions got the best of me. We have to control our emotions. Your rulings, Your Honour, have been consistent. You have said repeatedly, and others, and Judge Clark as well, have said repeatedly what the procedure was. And as evidence by Judge Clark today, I think -- I'm going to be very careful and not emotional myself when I say: It does try the courtroom's patience when the same conduct occurs day after day, no matter how many times the Rules been explained. I won't say more, Mr. President, but I believe we've conducted ourselves properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I've heard the views from both parties, and both Defence counsel suggested to us that they would like to submit the written objections. So we'll give you three days for your submission of your written objections on this document, and we'll make the decisions at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I just have a very short question to ask Mr. Scott in relation to the document, and it's probably been explained to me on a number of occasions, but I've forgotten. Did you explain, or did Mr. Prlic explain to us that the Zagreb archives stamp is one matter, but that the number is a numbering that's put on in the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Judge Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, in these circumstances, it surely wouldn't, Mr. Scott, be terribly difficult for someone in the OTP to find out what documents came before this, so Mr. Seric's and Mr. Meek's and Mr. Krsnik's very real concerns about the document could be assuaged, if it can be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me give this explanation, and I know it's late. I'm only responding Mr. President, because obviously I've been asked. I can check on the sequences, the numbers. To be perfectly honest, Judge Clark, that's not necessarily an indication of anything, because as documents are selected from the archive and brought back to The Hague to be further processed, it could be another document from another day could be given the numbering sequence right before this. And not every document -- certainly you can understand, I hope, we have not brought back every document from the archive or we'd have this building or certainly this room full of documents. I can inquire, I can inquire to see if it happens to be that there was some related document before this. Let me make it more specific, if it helps. I can tell the Chamber myself from prior occasions that when I review documents -- sometimes you may get a document immediately before this from a completely different collection. It was seized from a Serb collection in Banja Luka and it has the number right before this number. Having said that, I will inquire, but I'm not sure it will be -- I'm not sure it will assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: What I think that all your colleagues on the Defence side, and indeed I would like to know, is, the most important question is: Where did the document come from before it arrived in the archives? As Mr. Krsnik said, did it come from Sarajevo? Did it come from various other places? Did it actually come from the Heliodrom? It would be good to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I can -- again, Judge Clark, I'm happy to make a further inquiry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we will rise until 10 minutes past 4.00, and we'll have the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I can hear you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Can we hear each other? Yes. Before we begin our conversation, I would like to inform you that this Honourable Chamber has approved the measures of your protection and that during your today's examination your image, your voice, and your name will be protected. In front of you, you have a piece of paper, where your name is supposed to be written. If this is correct, your name, just say yes, without reading.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: In the course of this intercourse, we shall try to speak slowly, and we shall have to wait for each other after we have finished our respective speech. Pay attention to this red light on the microphone. When I finish my question, I will switch off the microphone and the red light will go off, and then you slowly start your answer. If necessary, I will just give you a signal with my hand to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, please, can we have a private session now? I would like to ask certain questions concerning the personality of the witness himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are now back in the open session, so please be careful not to mention your name during this intercourse, and I will also take care of that. My first question would be: During the Serbian aggression against Mostar, can you tell me what happened with you? And I'm especially interested to know whether you were militarily engaged during the Serbian aggression.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: During the Serbian aggression I was a member of the HOS unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us in auto few sentences how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: There's some problem with the questions and answers, because from the transcript, we cannot distinguish between questions and answers. So you have to make a pause, longer pause, after your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this warning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: My question was: Were you militarily engaged? You said you were a member of the HOS. Now my question is: Can you tell us in a few sentences how you joined the HOS, and in what manner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: I approached Mr. Martinovic. He immediately received me. I said I was available. I wasn't engaged anyplace else. And he admitted me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Are we talking about Vinko Martinovic, Stela?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did he hold any position in the HOS at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: He was a HOS commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you know Vinko Martinovic from earlier, and what was the nature of your acquaintanceship with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: I used to be a friend of his father's, and I still am. We were in the same business. We were -- his father and I were both taxi drivers. I came to their house on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit more? What was the ethnic composition of the HOS? Who were members of those units, of that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: Members of the HOS unit -- the composition was half and half, Muslims and Croats, and maybe two or three Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you tell me how long you stayed in the HOS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: Until the very end, the 8th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: After that -- which year?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Poriouvaev.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Just in order to clarify about the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you state which year that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: 1992. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thereafter, you left HOS, and then have you joined any other units after you abandoned HOS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: Immediately, the following day, I handed over my workshop to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: While you were a member of the HOS, did you do any work in the workshop? And what was your particular duty while you were in the HOS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: I worked on the repair of vehicles that were used by the HOS troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And now you said immediately, on the following day, you handed it over to the Army of the BH. Does that mean that you became a member of any units of the BH? And if that is the case, can you tell me which unit was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: That was the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: In the 4th Corps of the army BH, what was your duty, and where was physically this corps located? Where were you physically located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: The corps was on the Santiceva Street, and the workshop was very close to the Hotel Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: For the sake of orientation of this Chamber, can you tell us: Was it on the left bank or on the right bank of the Neretva, or in the so-called East or West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: In the Western Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: What were your duties in the unit and this workshop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: I did the same thing. I repaired the vehicles, irrespective of whether they belonged to the army or to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. I can't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: There's a problem. I saw your microphone is on, but the interpreters could not hear you. Maybe there's a problem of the channel. Will you try it again, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Mr. President. The last thing we see in the transcript is where you say you repaired vehicles, regardless of whether they belonged to the BH army or the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And my question was: What were the relations between the HVO and the BH army at the time, and whether they were acting together at the time in one way or another.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: Yes. The relations between them were very good, and at that time they acted jointly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: On the 9th of May, 1993, do you know what happened on that date? Was that day in any way remarkable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was a remarkable day, because that day I set off to work, unaware of what was going on in the town. I came near my workshop, when I was warned by a friend, uniformed. He was there at the checkpoint - that I should not proceed further, that it was very dangerous, that some kind of fighting had broken out between the BH army and the HVO because one of the Armija units was accommodated very near the workshop, that is in the hotel, and the SFOR was to pull it out from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And what happened then? Did you go home or did you go to the unit? Where did you spend the day? And did anything special happen to you that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: I returned home that same -- immediately, and I was in front of the building. I heard that there was some gunfire that evening. And from that day on, I could no longer get to my workshop.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: At the time, from then on, did you have any problems? Or, more specifically, were you arrested in some way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you, -- during the war, were you ever arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: No, not until the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And what happened on the 30th of June, 1993? What happened to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: On the 30th of June, that day, the Northern Camp fell, and the Radio Mostar, on the left bank, commander Arif Pasalic, spoke on Mostar Radio and he requested that all the Muslims on the right bank offer resistance to the HVO, and I realised then that something strange would happen. And so it did, around 4.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Before you tell us what specifically happened, can you tell us: Arif Pasalic, you said, was a commander. Of which army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: The Army of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: The Army of BH. So therefore you expected that something was to happen. You heard this message addressed to you, the Muslims. So what happened at 4.00?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: After lunch, I took a nap, and then about 4.00 my wife and a friend of mine, she woke us up. She saw the military police in the compound -- around the building, and she saw people coming out of the buildings. They were standing in a file, two by two. And she noticed that they were being taken away to some place. She didn't know exactly where. I only managed to have a cup a coffee. A young man knocked at the door and said to me and my friend to get ready, to bring a few things, some warm clothes with us, and that is how I set off.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Tell me: Did you at that time, on that date -- were still a member of the Army of BH?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So you went off with the military police. Who else was brought by the military police? What kind of group was that? How many of you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: There were between 35 and 40 men fit for military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Tell me: At the time, in your flat, did your son live there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: Yes, and one of my sons, the elder one, who was very sturdily built for his age, the young man who came to fetch us, he also said we should get ready. And then my wife produced his birth certificate and showed it to this military policeman and he sent him back.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Therefore, they didn't think that he was fit for military service, therefore he wasn't taken with you. Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: They put us on a bus and drove us to Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So can we see -- hear again which day it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: 30th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: While you were at the Heliodrom, were you mistreated and abused in any way? Did anything in particular happen to you at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: No, nothing. We just went to an office, where they registered us, and then they put us into a gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you tell me: Were you taken on the subsequent days from the Heliodrom to perform labour for certain military units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: On the 30th of June, 1993, when I was taken away, I said to my wife to ask a neighbour of ours to go to Vinko Martinovic, Stela, and to try to pull me out, because he had promised me that when we met in early June. He was in a car, in the company of Sejo Huskovic. He stopped the car and we had a conversation. And in view of the situation that prevailed in the town, I asked him if he was willing to help me if it should happen that -- if something happened to me. He promised me, and for that reason I instructed my wife to go to his family, to find him and ask him to do something for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Do you know whether your wife had gone to see him, what happened, and how did you -- did you and how did you ever find out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: My wife told me that our neighbour, Rade Culjak, took her to his house. He wasn't at home. His parents were there. They listened to her, but they couldn't do anything, or they couldn't promise anything. So she went back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Do you know whether this request of your wife, did it ever reach Stela, and did Stela ever, in any way, react to your request?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: The only thing I know is that on the 6th or the seventh day when at the Heliodrom, I received a message from my wife, through a soldier, to keep an eye on a blue truck, Deutz truck that was supposed to arrive, that I should report to this group, and that this truck was supposed to take people to Stela.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you act in accordance with this instruction, this message? Did you see this blue truck? Did you reach Stela's unit, and how?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: Quite simply, they wanted to single out 20 men to go to work. I stood in the line, boarded the truck, and we were driven to the base of Mr. Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us: What was -- when was it that you went to Stela's for the first time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: It could have been 6th, 7th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I -- oh, yes. I see. It says 6th or 7th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So you were for the first time in Stela's unit. What does it look like? Did you see Stela there? How did you fare that first day? What was the situation like in that base?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: When we got off the truck, we again lined up two and two, and Mr. Martinovic spotted me. He immediately singled me out, took me to the side, me and two others, and then he took us to the office, where we sat down, had some coffee, talked. And he said that he could not do anything for me earlier, that that was the only way. So we sat there for about 45 minutes, or perhaps an hour, and then one of the soldiers came in, and he said to Martinovic to take me home immediately, whether he could take me home. And he allowed it and then he took me home, perhaps sometime around 9.00. I spent the whole day at home and at 6.00 he came again to take me back to the base.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. When you say "home," I understand it is your home, your family, your wife and children, and then he took you back to the base. Very well. But after that, after that first day, did you continue going to that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: Yes. I went there almost every day except when the soldiers at the Heliodrom, the guards, would notice that I had arrived clean, and after having had a bath, and then they would object to Mr. Martinovic for letting me home. And then for two or three days, he wouldn't -- they wouldn't let me go to work for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So it was by your physical appearance that they drew the conclusions that you had been home and not working?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you now tell me and the Court: How many days, all told, did you spend at the Heliodrom? For how many days were you a prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: About 72 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Of those 72 days, how many days did you spend with that unit, at Vinko Martinovic's?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: Forty-five to fifty days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Tell me: Did you sometimes spend a night with that unit. Someone's place, perhaps to the front line or somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Does that mean that you volunteered for come and stay in that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: Yes, it happened on various occasions, two, three, sometimes even five nights.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And of those fifty days that you spent there, for how many days would it account, when you had to stay there overnight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: About twenty days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you explain it to us somehow, how is it-- how did Vinko Martinovic manage to do it? To keep you there overnight? How could he keep you there, so you wouldn't have to go back to the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: Well, nothing. Except on the paper we said whop had-- was returned to the Heliodrom. He just wrote there that I spend the night there for some reason or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: But did you stay there overnight because you wanted that or because they needed you there because there was some work to be done?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: There only reason was because I used that moment-- had I gone back to the Heliodrom in the morning perhaps I would be taken to some worse place. Perhaps to the front line or somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Does it mean that you volunteered to come and stay in that unit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: We've lost about two minutes of transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Witness, we'll have to repeat some of the questions, because something happened to the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Par. Whether it's just my monitor or everybody's else's it's stopped at: Tell me: Did you sometimes spend a night with that unit? Did he, and it stops there. And it hasn't continued on my monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. My monitor is the same. Yes, absolutely the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Was I the only one listening?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm listening too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Par, can I -- for this and ask you to ask the witness to slow down because sometimes he must remember that it has to be interpreted for the rest of us, and he's for a -- too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we were told that we need about five minutes to fix it up, so could we make a break at this time and we'll resume at 5.00, five-minutes' break. --- Break taken at 4.54 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Par, please continue, or repeat your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Witness, you could see we had some technical problems, and we shall have to repeat some of the questions. So let us take up from my question when I asked you how many days did you spend at the Heliodrom all told. You told us 72 days. Then I asked you how many days did you spend with the unit at Vinko Martinovic, Stela's, and you said: "I think 45 days." After that, my question was, and now I will ask you to answer: Did you ever spend the night with the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: Yes, I did, on various occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us: How many days, roughly, did you stay overnight, of those 45, 50 days, how many nights did you spend there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: About 20 nights.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Tell me: Did you stay there of your own will or did you have certain duties to perform overnight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: No. I had no obligations, no duties to perform overnight, but in this way I avoided the Heliodrom, so that I wouldn't have to go to some worse place, perhaps the confrontation line, the next morning, or perhaps so that I wouldn't have to do some heavier work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. And how did Vinko Martinovic manage to explain it to the Heliodrom? Why did he have to keep you overnight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: Quite simply, he would write on a piece of paper the unit needs him, and that is how we stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did other prisoners also stay overnight or were you the only one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: Well, almost every night, four, five, maybe even six, would stay there overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And did the same situation apply to them? Did they ask to stay there? Did they stay of their own free will?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: They stayed there of their own free will.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And can you tell us briefly: Where did you sleep? What were the conditions there when you stayed the night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: We slept on the upper floor, in the base, in beds. There was a living room there which we could use.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Were you locked up? Were you kept under guard on those occasions when you stayed there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: No, we were not locked up. And there was always an elderly home guard who would spend the night there to guard the base, and we could go out and talk with him. If you didn't feel like sleeping, so we chatted. I didn't feel like I was being guarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. You spent a lot of time with that unit, so will you now answer some questions concerning the conditions in the unit. And please, I will ask you to tell us about yourself first. Tell me: What were the jobs that you were asked to do in the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: Well, I was mostly involved in preparing vehicles that the members of the unit used.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And those jobs, did you do them under coercion? Were you forced to do it or did you volunteer to do them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: Well, they knew that I was a mechanic, so they turned to me. No, I didn't do it under compulsion; I did it voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any remuneration for the work that you did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: Well, as a rule, I did. Sometimes I did some small things, and perhaps it was not worth paying. But every soldiers, if nothing else, brought me a package of cigarettes too, or gave me some money.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And tell me: What about your meals? Where did you get your meals at the time that you were with the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: In the unit, in daytime, we would get some dry pack; and in the evening we brought the food from a restaurant which was nearby, which was near the base.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Could you tell us: What was that restaurant called?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: Hladovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Tell me: During your stay there, did you receive any visits? How often did you go home, if, that is, you went home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: I had no need to have any visitors because I went home to see my family almost every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And how did you go to see your family? Did you go there on your own or in some other way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: As a rule, a soldier would take me home and then come again to fetch me at the agreed time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Right. So that is how you fared. But I guess there were some other prisoners, and what about them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: Well, what I could see, because I wasn't there all the time, I would be home or I don't know. And the majority of them enjoyed almost the same treatment as I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you see any mistreatment of prisoners or their degradation, their humiliation in some way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Tell me: Were you ever sent to the separation line next to the health centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: Yes, but only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Could you tell us about it? When did you go? Where did you go? What did you do there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: It was once, when a soldier was killed, and he was to be buried. We were three or four of us in the headquarters, and every funeral passed by the headquarters. And then Mr. Martinovic suggested that we should go to the front line ourselves because we would be the safest there, because there were people in the procession who would be walking on foot, and in order to avoid some incident. So we went to the line, as advised by Mr. Martinovic, and we were really safe there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I see. So it was for your safety. Tell us: Did you go there on your own, without any military escort? And how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MI
utterances.text: We went there on our own and stayed there an hour, an hour and a half. I don't know how long the funeral lasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
